Text: The Arabic alphabet contains {{c1::twenty-eight}} letters — consonants and long vowels — plus {{c2::fourteen}} symbols that act as short vowels, pronunciation markers, or grammatical markers.
Back Extra: Cue: letters carry the skeleton; the symbol layer rides above and below it.

Text: The four major characteristics that set Arabic script apart from European ones: {{c1::it is written right to left}}; {{c1::letters connect in both print and script}}; {{c1::letters change shape by position (initial / medial / final)}}; {{c1::the script has two layers — a consonant-and-long-vowel skeleton, plus the vowelling}}.
Back Extra: Cue: four — direction, connection, position, layers.

Text: Arabic is written and read from {{c1::right to left}}.
Back Extra: Cue: books and magazines open the "other way" from English ones.

Text: Arabic letters are connected {{c1::in both print AND script}} — unlike Latin letters, which connect only in handwriting.
Back Extra: Why: this is why letters change shape by position — they must join their neighbors.

Text: "{{c1::Initial}} position" = the letter is not connected to a previous letter; "{{c2::medial}} position" = the letter sits between two other letters.
Back Extra: Cue: Unit 1 teaches only the independent (isolated) forms — position variants come in Units 2-10.

Text: The basic skeleton of an Arabic word is made of {{c1::the consonants and long vowels}}; short vowels and other markers are {{c1::a separate layer}} written above and below it.
Back Extra: Cue: two layers — skeleton first, vowelling second.

Text: The vowelling layer (vocalization) is normally {{c1::omitted}} in written Arabic — readers recognize words {{c1::without it}}.
Back Extra: Pitfall: your textbook prints vowels while you learn; newspapers will not.

Text: The Arabic writing system is regularly {{c1::phonetic}}: a one-to-one correspondence between sound and letter — words are written {{c1::the way they are pronounced}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: English spelling is the opposite — think though / tough / through.

Text: In this book's transliteration, emphatic sounds are marked by {{c1::UPPERCASE letters (S vs s)}}, and long vowels by {{c1::doubled vowels (aa, ii, uu)}}.
Back Extra: Ex: S = emphatic ص while s = plain س; aa is held longer than a.

Text: Transliteration is used only for words containing {{c1::letters you have not yet learned}} — and it does not replace {{c1::listening to the audio}}.
Back Extra: Cue: the book drops transliteration for a word once its letters are all taught.

Text: Formal Arabic has only {{c1::three::how many}} vowel qualities — {{c1::a, i, u}} — each short or long; spoken Arabic adds {{c2::e and o}}.
Back Extra: Cue: vowel length distinguishes emphatic consonants from their plain counterparts — listen for it.
verified_against: p26 text layer + vowel chart render

Text: Levantine pronunciation sometimes uses a very short, unstressed {{c1::schwa}} sound (ə).
Back Extra: Ex: the e in listen.

Text: Formal Arabic — also called {{c1::Modern Standard}} or {{c1::Classical}} Arabic — is learned {{c2::at school (not at home)}} and is more a {{c2::written}} register than a spoken one.
Back Extra: Cue: you hear it on news broadcasts; educated speakers mix it with dialect in formal settings.

Text: The {{c1::Levantine}} dialect group covers the Syrian, Lebanese, Palestinian, and Jordanian dialects.
Back Extra: Cue: the Levant = the eastern Mediterranean coast region.

Text: This book's two colloquial varieties: shaami = {{c1::Levantine}}, and maSri = {{c1::Egyptian}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: shaami can mean Syrian, Damascene, or Levantine.

Cue: the dialogues use one city's flavor of each — see the sibling card.
verified_against: p28 text layer + Lingco lesson 8174 intro

Text: The book's shaami dialogues use the dialect of {{c1::Damascus}}; its maSri is the dialect of {{c2::Cairo}}.
Back Extra: Cue: one city stands in for each dialect group.

Text: Egyptian (maSri) pronunciation is marked by a hard {{c1::g}} where other dialects say j, and by stress on the {{c1::second-to-last}} syllable.
Back Extra: Ex: gamiil for jamiil.

Text: Levantine dialects are marked by a final {{c1::e}} vowel on certain nouns/adjectives where other dialects have a, and by a distinctive {{c1::intonation}}.
Back Extra: Ex: Levantine ahla vs formal ahlan.

Text: Polite behavior requires you to say hello to {{c1::everyone in a room or place you enter}} — including a loosely defined {{c1::"space" someone regularly occupies}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: an outdoor work area, or a guard's position outside a building.

Cue: entering = greeting; the room does not have to have walls.
